Chapter 3: Letting Go of Old Habits and Expectations
Change has this uncanny way of shining a light on the habits and expectations we once clung to—the ones that felt so essential, yet now, seem to hold us back.
When the tried-and-true routines stop working, it’s so tempting to just double down, isn’t it? To hold on tighter, to pour even more energy into what used to bring us comfort. But sooner or later, we’re faced with a simple truth: some things need to be released, just to make room for what’s next.
Imagine someone who always found their sense of security in achievements—those good grades, job promotions, all the praise from others. Then, suddenly, life throws a curveball. Maybe it’s a move to a brand-new city, and just like that, all those familiar ways of feeling accomplished are gone. At first, it’s easy to fall into frantic mode—volunteering for every committee, signing up for classes, filling every blank spot on the calendar. But before long, the exhaustion creeps in. Then comes that quiet, sometimes uncomfortable realization: the old ways of measuring success just don’t fit anymore.
Letting go isn’t usually a one-time decision. It’s more like a journey, marked by lots of little acts of release. For some, it means stepping away from commitments that just don’t spark joy anymore. For others, it’s allowing themselves to actually rest—without guilt—even if that to-do list is still glaring at them. There might be moments of real grief, too—letting go of an identity built on busyness, or missing the comfort of always being needed. But with that release comes relief—a sense of lightness, like you’ve finally set down a burden you were never meant to carry forever.
And here’s where the unexpected gifts begin to show up. With fewer obligations, suddenly there’s time for real connection—a long walk with someone you love, a lazy morning with coffee, or those unhurried chats with your kids. The pressure to constantly achieve fades, and space opens up for deeper relationships and a more honest version of yourself. It becomes clear: your worth isn’t tied to how productive you are, or how many boxes you check off—it’s about being present, and being real.
A lot of us hesitate to let go because we worry it means we’ve failed. What if life falls apart without those old habits and expectations? But the thing is, letting go is actually the first step toward something new. It’s an act of trust—a belief that something good can grow in the space that’s left behind.
Over time, letting go starts to feel less like losing something, and more like gaining freedom. It doesn’t mean giving up on responsibility or ambition. It’s about choosing what really matters right now. The old ways worked for a season, but new seasons call for new ways of being. And in this open space, there’s real room for growth, for discovery, and—maybe best of all—for a deeper sense of peace.
